modules.summary: Machine learning in context, then transformers and attention at architect depth.

lessons.title: Machine Learning in Context — What an Architect Needs
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The honest scope

You do not need to derive backpropagation. You do need to know which class of problem a technique solves, what it needs to work, and how it fails — because those are the questions that arrive in design reviews.

## The categories

**Supervised learning** — labelled examples in, prediction out. Classification and regression. Needs labels, which are usually the expensive part.

**Unsupervised learning** — structure without labels. Clustering, dimensionality reduction. Embeddings come from this family.

**Reinforcement learning** — learning from reward signals. Relevant to you mainly because RLHF is how base models are turned into instruction-following assistants.

**Deep learning** — many-layered neural networks. Transformers are the architecture that made modern language models work.

## Training, fine-tuning, prompting, retrieval

Four ways to get a model to do what you want, in ascending order of cost:

1. **Prompting** — no training. Instant, cheap, iterate in seconds. Start here, always.
2. **Retrieval (RAG)** — supply the facts at inference time. Handles changing knowledge, gives citations, no training.
3. **Fine-tuning** — adjust weights on your examples. Teaches *behaviour and format*, not facts. Needs hundreds to thousands of quality examples and a maintenance commitment.
4. **Pre-training** — building a base model. Not something an enterprise does.

The single most common expensive mistake is fine-tuning to inject knowledge. Fine-tuning changes how a model responds; it does not reliably add facts, and those facts go stale with no way to update them short of retraining. Knowledge belongs in retrieval.

## How it fails

Models generate plausible text, not true text. They have no notion of confidence in the way a database does. They degrade over long contexts, and they change when the vendor updates them. Every one of those is an architectural constraint to design around, not a bug to be fixed with a better prompt.
keyTakeaways: Fine-tuning teaches behaviour; retrieval supplies facts — never swap them
Always start with prompting; it costs minutes instead of weeks
Models generate plausible text, not true text, and have no database-style confidence
Model behaviour changes when the vendor updates — pin versions and re-evaluate

lessons.title: Transformers, Attention and Why Context Costs Money
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Attention, briefly

A transformer processes every token in relation to every other token. "Attention" is the mechanism that scores which other tokens matter when interpreting each one — that is how the model resolves what "it" refers to three sentences back.

The architectural consequence: attention is roughly quadratic in sequence length. Doubling the context does not double the compute, it roughly quadruples the attention component. This is why long-context requests are slower and more expensive than a linear reading of the price list suggests, and why "just put everything in the context window" is not a strategy.

## Tokens

Models see tokens, not words or characters. Roughly, English averages about four characters per token, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words. Code tokenises less efficiently. Non-English text often tokenises much less efficiently — sometimes two or three times worse, which is a real cost factor for multilingual systems and one that surprises people.

Everything is priced per token, input and output separately, usually with output costing several times more than input.

## Context windows

The context window bounds system prompt + conversation history + retrieved documents + the response, together. A large window is not free capacity — it is a budget you spend.

And filling it degrades quality. Models reliably attend to the beginning and end of a long context while losing material in the middle — the "lost in the middle" effect. Twenty well-chosen chunks routinely beat a hundred mediocre ones, both in cost and in answer quality. That single fact drives most of RAG design.

## What this means architecturally

Context is a scarce, priced resource. Budget it explicitly: a fixed allocation for the system prompt, a bounded allocation for history, a bounded allocation for retrieval, and a reserve for the response. Put the most important material last, where attention is strongest.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  CW[Context window: 128k tokens] --> SP[System prompt ~800]
  CW --> H[History, capped 8k]
  CW --> R[Retrieved chunks\nthe variable part]
  CW --> RES[Reserved for response 4k]
  R --> Q{More chunks?}
  Q -->|Yes| COST[Higher cost + mid-context loss]
  Q -->|Fewer, better| BEST[Lower cost + better answers]
keyTakeaways: Attention is roughly quadratic in sequence length — long context costs more than linear pricing suggests
About 4 characters per token in English; code and non-English tokenise worse
Models lose material in the middle of long contexts: 20 good chunks beat 100 mediocre ones
Budget the context explicitly and put the most important material last

modules.title: Embeddings and Vector Similarity
modules.summary: What an embedding is, what cosine similarity measures, and where vectors quietly fail.

lessons.title: Embeddings and Vector Similarity, Properly Understood
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What an embedding is

A fixed-length array of floats — typically 768, 1,536 or 3,072 dimensions — positioned so that text with similar meaning lands nearby. "Cancel my subscription" and "how do I end my membership" have no words in common and sit close together. That is the entire value proposition.

## Cosine similarity

The angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude. Ranges from -1 to 1; in practice with modern text embeddings almost everything falls between about 0.3 and 0.95, which is why absolute thresholds are unreliable and relative ranking is what you use.

## The failure modes that matter

**Negation.** "The policy covers flood damage" and "the policy does not cover flood damage" embed close together. Semantically they are opposites; the vector space barely distinguishes them. For anything where negation carries meaning — legal, medical, insurance — pure vector search is dangerous and hybrid search is not optional.

**Exact identifiers.** Product codes, invoice numbers, error codes, names. Vectors are poor at these. Keyword search is excellent at them. This is the second reason hybrid retrieval wins.

**Domain mismatch.** A model embedded on general web text will underperform on dense domain jargon. Sometimes visibly, sometimes just quietly worse.

## Practical rules

- Query and document must use the **same** embedding model. Mixing them produces silently meaningless results.
- Changing the embedding model means reindexing everything. Budget for it; it is not a configuration flip.
- Larger dimensions cost more storage and search time for often marginal quality gains. Measure before paying.
- Normalise vectors once at write time so search does dot products instead of full cosine calculations.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  T[Text] --> E[Embedding model]
  E --> V[Vector of 1536 floats]
  V --> N[Normalise at write time]
  N --> IDX[(Vector index)]
  Q[Query] --> E2[Same embedding model]
  E2 --> S[Similarity search]
  S --> IDX
  IDX --> R[Ranked results]
keyTakeaways: Embeddings capture meaning, which is why paraphrases match without shared words
Negation is a genuine blind spot: opposites can score above 0.9
Vectors are poor at exact identifiers — keyword search covers that gap
Query and documents must use the same model; changing it means a full reindex

lessons.title: Vector Databases: Azure AI Search, pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The options, and who they suit

**Azure AI Search** — the default in an Azure enterprise. Vector plus keyword plus semantic reranking in one service, with security filters, faceting and managed identity integration. You are not assembling three systems to get hybrid search.

**PostgreSQL + pgvector** — vectors in the database you already run. One system to operate, back up and secure; transactional consistency between your data and your vectors. Excellent up to a few million vectors on adequate hardware. Available in Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Aurora.

**Pinecone** — managed, purpose-built, scales to very large corpora without you thinking about index maintenance. Another vendor, another bill, another data location question for your compliance team.

**Qdrant** — open source, self-hostable or managed, strong filtering, good performance. Sensible when data residency rules out a US-hosted SaaS.

## The honest default

If you are already on Azure and need hybrid search with security trimming, use Azure AI Search. If you already run PostgreSQL and have fewer than a few million chunks, use pgvector and avoid adding a system. Reach for a dedicated vector database when you have a specific scale or feature requirement that the first two cannot meet — and be able to name it.

## Indexes

HNSW is the common choice: fast approximate search, higher memory. IVFFlat uses less memory and needs training on representative data. Both are **approximate** — you are trading a small amount of recall for a large amount of speed, and you should know roughly how much.

## What actually decides it

Not benchmark throughput. It is: does it do hybrid search, can it filter by security metadata efficiently, where does the data live, and who operates it at 3am.
lessons.codeExample:
-- pgvector: vectors alongside the relational data, in one transaction.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE document_chunks (
    id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    document_id  UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    chunk_index  INT         NOT NULL,
    content      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    -- Written at ingestion so retrieval filters by entitlement in SQL,
    -- not by asking the model nicely.
    allowed_groups TEXT[]    NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    page_number  INT,
    embedding    vector(1536) NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- HNSW: fast approximate search. Build after bulk load, not before.
CREATE INDEX ON document_chunks
    USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

-- Supports the permission filter efficiently.
CREATE INDEX ON document_chunks USING gin (allowed_groups);

-- Full-text column for the keyword half of hybrid search.
ALTER TABLE document_chunks
    ADD COLUMN content_tsv tsvector
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX ON document_chunks USING gin (content_tsv);

-- Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, permissions applied in SQL.
WITH vector_hits AS (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rank
    FROM document_chunks
    WHERE allowed_groups && $2::text[]
    ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
    LIMIT 50
),
keyword_hits AS (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        ORDER BY ts_rank(content_tsv, plainto_tsquery('english', $3)) DESC) AS rank
    FROM document_chunks
    WHERE content_tsv @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $3)
      AND allowed_groups && $2::text[]
    LIMIT 50
)
SELECT c.id, c.content, c.page_number,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + v.rank), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0) AS score
FROM document_chunks c
LEFT JOIN vector_hits  v ON v.id = c.id
LEFT JOIN keyword_hits k ON k.id = c.id
WHERE v.id IS NOT NULL OR k.id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 20;
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  Q{Which vector store?} --> A[Already on Azure,\nneed hybrid + security trimming]
  Q --> B[Already run PostgreSQL,\nunder ~5M chunks]
  Q --> C[Very large scale,\nfully managed]
  Q --> D[Data residency rules out\nUS-hosted SaaS]
  A --> AIS[Azure AI Search]
  B --> PG[PostgreSQL + pgvector]
  C --> PC[Pinecone]
  D --> QD[Qdrant self-hosted]
keyTakeaways: Azure AI Search is the default in an Azure enterprise: hybrid search and security trimming built in
pgvector avoids adding a system and gives transactional consistency up to a few million chunks
HNSW and IVFFlat are approximate — know the recall you are trading away
Hybrid search and efficient permission filtering decide the choice, not raw throughput

modules.title: Model Selection and Evaluation
modules.summary: Choosing a model on evidence, and knowing whether a change made things better or worse.

lessons.title: Model Selection: Capability, Latency and Cost
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Three axes, always in tension

Capability, latency, cost. Frontier models are the most capable, slowest and most expensive. Small models are fast and cheap and fail on harder reasoning. There is no single right answer, only a right answer for a specific task.

## Routing rather than choosing

Mature systems route. Classification, extraction, simple summarisation and routing decisions go to a small model. Complex reasoning, architecture-style analysis and nuanced writing go to a large one. A well-designed router commonly cuts cost by half or more with no user-visible quality change, because most requests in a real system are not hard.

Implement routing behind an interface so the policy is configuration, not a deployment.

## Practical selection criteria

- **Task fit** — measure on *your* data, not a public leaderboard. Leaderboards measure someone else's problem.
- **Latency** — time to first token matters more than total time for interactive use. A fast first token feels responsive even when total generation is slower.
- **Context window** — must fit your worst case, not your average.
- **Structured output** — native JSON schema support is worth a lot in an enterprise pipeline.
- **Data residency** — often decides the question outright before anything else is considered.
- **Version stability** — pin the version. A silent vendor update that changes behaviour is a production incident with no deployment to blame.

## Always abstract the provider

Models change every few months. If your orchestration code imports a vendor SDK directly, every change is a migration. One interface, several implementations, model choice in configuration.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  R[Request] --> T{Task type}
  T -->|Classify / extract / summarise| S[Small fast model]
  T -->|Complex reasoning| L[Large model]
  T -->|Input over threshold| L
  S --> OK[Response]
  L --> OK
  S -.transient failure.-> F[Fallback provider]
  L -.transient failure.-> F
keyTakeaways: Route by task: small models handle most real traffic at a fraction of the cost
Measure on your own data — public leaderboards measure someone else's problem
Time to first token drives perceived speed in interactive use
Pin model versions and keep the provider behind an interface

lessons.title: Evaluating AI Systems
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The problem evaluation solves

An AI system degrades silently. No exception is thrown when answers get subtly worse. Without evaluation you find out from users, weeks later, and you cannot tell which of the last twelve changes caused it.

This is the single largest gap between teams that ship AI successfully and teams that ship demos.

## Build the evaluation set first

Before tuning anything, write 30 to 50 question/answer pairs drawn from real usage, covering the common cases, the hard cases and the cases where the correct response is a refusal. That set is now your regression suite.

It does not need to be large. It needs to be representative and stable.

## What to measure

**Retrieval** — recall at k (is the right document retrieved at all?) and precision. If retrieval fails, nothing downstream can save the answer.

**Generation** — groundedness (is every claim supported by the retrieved context?), relevance (does it answer the question?), and refusal correctness (does it decline when it should?).

**Operational** — p50 and p95 latency, cost per query, error rate.

## Judging

Three levels, in ascending order of cost and fidelity:

1. **Deterministic checks** — valid JSON, citation present, refusal when the context is empty, required fields populated. Cheap, fast, run on every commit.
2. **Model-as-judge** — a model scores groundedness against the retrieved context. Scalable, imperfect, good for relative comparison between releases.
3. **Human review** — a sample each release. Slow, expensive, and the only real ground truth.

Use all three. Deterministic checks in CI, model-as-judge as the release gate, human review on a sample.

## Gate the pipeline

Run the evaluation set on every change to prompts, models, chunking or retrieval, and fail the build when the score drops beyond a threshold. Without a gate, quality regressions ship, because nothing else in your pipeline can see them.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  CH[Change: prompt, model,\nchunking or retrieval] --> EV[Run evaluation set]
  EV --> R1[Retrieval recall]
  EV --> R2[Groundedness]
  EV --> R3[Refusal accuracy]
  EV --> R4[Latency and cost]
  R1 --> G{Within threshold\nof last release?}
  R2 --> G
  R3 --> G
  R4 --> G
  G -->|Yes| SHIP[Ship]
  G -->|No| BLOCK[Fail the build]
keyTakeaways: AI systems degrade silently — no exception is thrown when answers get worse
Build a 30–50 case evaluation set before tuning anything; it becomes your regression suite
Measure retrieval separately from generation: retrieval failure cannot be fixed downstream
Gate the pipeline on the evaluation score, or quality regressions ship unnoticed

modules.title: Provider Integration and Streaming
modules.summary: One abstraction over four providers, and streaming that behaves under failure.

lessons.title: A Provider Abstraction over OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why this is the first thing you build

You will change providers. A price change, an outage, a compliance decision, a new model that is better at your task — any of these forces it. If provider SDK types appear in your orchestration code, each change is a migration project.

One interface, several implementations, and the choice lives in configuration.

## What belongs in the abstraction

The common surface: messages with roles, system instructions, temperature and max tokens, tool definitions, streaming, and usage reporting. Keep it narrow — an abstraction that exposes every provider-specific option is not an abstraction.

Where providers genuinely differ, normalise: Anthropic takes the system prompt as a top-level parameter while OpenAI treats it as a message; tool-call shapes differ; token counting differs. That normalisation is precisely the value the adapter adds.

## Resilience is part of the contract

Every provider rate-limits and every provider has outages. The abstraction is where retry with exponential backoff, honouring `Retry-After`, and circuit breaking belong. Use `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` rather than hand-rolling it.

One non-obvious point: retry only on 429 and 5xx. Retrying a 400 just repeats the same malformed request, three times, at the same cost.

## Usage reporting is not optional

Every response must carry prompt tokens, completion tokens and computed cost. If that is not in the interface, cost monitoring will be bolted on later at three times the effort.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  APP[Application code] --> I[ILlmProvider]
  I --> A[AzureOpenAiProvider]
  I --> B[OpenAiProvider]
  I --> C[AnthropicProvider]
  I --> D[GeminiProvider]
  A --> R[Retry + circuit breaker]
  B --> R
  C --> R
  D --> R
  R --> U[Usage and cost reported\non every response]
keyTakeaways: Provider SDK types belong in exactly one adapter class, never in orchestration code
Normalise the genuine differences: system prompt placement, tool shapes, token counting
Retry only 429 and 5xx — retrying a 400 repeats the same broken request at the same cost
Put token usage and cost in the response contract from the first commit

lessons.title: Streaming to the Browser with Cancellation That Works
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why streaming is a requirement, not a nicety

A 2,000-token response takes 15 to 30 seconds to generate. Delivered as one block, that is an unusable interface. Streamed, the first token appears in under a second and the experience feels immediate even though total time is unchanged.

## Server-sent events

SSE is the right transport here: one-directional, plain HTTP, automatic browser reconnection, no WebSocket infrastructure. `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` maps onto it naturally in ASP.NET Core.

The details that bite:

- Disable response buffering, or the whole point is lost to a reverse proxy holding the output.
- Send heartbeat comments during long pauses, or intermediaries close an idle connection.
- Flush after every chunk.

## Cancellation genuinely matters

When the user closes the tab, `HttpContext.RequestAborted` fires. Propagate it into the provider call. Without this you keep generating — and keep paying for — tokens nobody will read. On a busy system this is a measurable share of the bill.

## Failing mid-stream

This is the case teams forget. Once you have sent a 200 and started streaming, you cannot send an error status. Define an error event type in the protocol and have the client render partial content plus a clear failure indicator. Test it deliberately, because it will happen.

## Persisting what was streamed

Accumulate the streamed content server-side and persist it when the stream completes — including on cancellation, where partial content is usually still worth keeping. Relying on the client to send the assembled message back is both slower and untrustworthy.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|POST /stream| API[ASP.NET Core]
  API --> P[LLM provider]
  P -->|token| API
  API -->|event: token| B
  P -->|token| API
  API -->|event: token| B
  API -->|event: done + usage| B
  B -.close tab.-> CAN[RequestAborted]
  CAN --> STOP[Stop generating,\nstop paying, save partial]
keyTakeaways: SSE plus IAsyncEnumerable is the natural fit; disable buffering and flush every chunk
Propagate RequestAborted into the provider call or you pay for tokens nobody reads
After a 200 you cannot send an error status — define an error event and test it
Accumulate and persist server-side, including on cancellation

modules.title: Structured Outputs and Tool Calling
modules.summary: Making model output safe to parse, and letting a model act without letting it decide what it may do.

lessons.title: Structured Outputs and JSON Schemas
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The problem

"Respond in JSON" works nine times out of ten. In production, one failure in ten is an incident. Models add explanatory prose, wrap output in markdown fences, or invent an enum value that your parser has never heard of.

## Native structured output

Modern models support a JSON schema on the request and constrain generation to satisfy it. Where available this is dramatically more reliable than prompting, because the constraint operates during decoding rather than as a request.

The constraints worth knowing: every property typically must be required, `additionalProperties` must be false, and deeply nested or recursive schemas may be rejected. Design flat schemas.

## Validate anyway

Schema-constrained generation guarantees shape, not sense. A date can be well-formed and absurd. A confidence value can be a valid float and meaningless. Validate business rules after parsing, always.

## Designing schemas the model handles well

- Flat beats nested. Deep structures produce more failures.
- Enums beat free text for anything you will branch on.
- Name fields descriptively: `invoiceTotalIncludingTax` outperforms `amt`.
- Include a confidence field and an explicit `"unknown"` option — otherwise the model must guess, and it will.

That last point is the one most teams miss. If the schema offers no way to express uncertainty, you have required the model to fabricate.

## When schema support is absent

Fall back to prompting with an example, then strip markdown fences, parse, and on failure retry once with the parse error included in the prompt. Give up after two attempts rather than looping.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  D[Document] --> L[LLM with JSON schema]
  L --> P{Parses?}
  P -->|No, attempt 1| RT[Retry with the parse error]
  RT --> L
  P -->|Yes| V{Business rules pass?}
  V -->|No, attempt 1| RT
  V -->|Yes| OK[Accept]
  P -->|No, attempt 2| HR[Human review]
  V -->|No, attempt 2| HR
keyTakeaways: Native JSON schema support constrains generation and is far more reliable than asking nicely
Schema compliance guarantees shape, never sense — validate business rules afterwards
Always give the model a way to express uncertainty, or you have required it to guess
Retry once with the specific error, then route to human review

lessons.title: Tool Calling with Server-Side Authorisation
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The mental model that keeps you safe

The model does not call your tools. The model **requests** a call; your code decides whether to make it. Everything about tool-calling security follows from holding that distinction firmly.

Treat a tool call request exactly as you would treat an HTTP request from an untrusted client — because that is what it is.

## Authorise against the user, not the model

The tool request arrives with arguments the model chose. Those arguments are attacker-influenceable via the conversation. So:

- Bind every tool execution to the authenticated principal from the request context.
- Never let the model supply the identity. If the tool needs a customer ID, take it from the session, or verify the supplied one against the caller's entitlements.
- Validate arguments against the schema, then against business rules.

The canonical failure: a `get_customer_orders(customerId)` tool that trusts the argument. A user asks "show me orders for customer 4471" and reads someone else's data. The model did nothing wrong; the authorisation was missing.

## Designing tools well

- Few, well-named tools beat many overlapping ones. Models choose badly among near-duplicates.
- Descriptions are prompts — say when to use the tool *and when not to*.
- Return structured results with an explicit error shape, so a failure is something the model can reason about rather than a mystery.
- Keep tools fast. Every call is a round trip plus another inference.

## Bounding the loop

Model requests tool, you execute, result goes back, model may request another. Always cap the iterations, apply a wall-clock timeout, and cap total tokens. An unbounded agent loop is an unbounded invoice.
keyTakeaways: The model requests; your code decides. Treat every tool call as an untrusted request
Authorise the tool AND its arguments against the authenticated user
Return structured errors the model can reason about, never raw exceptions
Cap iterations, wall-clock time and total tokens — an unbounded loop is an unbounded bill

modules.title: Prompts, Memory and Context Management
modules.summary: System prompts as versioned artefacts, and conversation memory inside a token budget.

lessons.title: System Prompts as Versioned Artefacts
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Prompts are code

A prompt that determines how your system behaves is code. Treat it accordingly: version it, review it, test it, and record which version produced which response.

When answer quality drops in production, the first question is "what changed?" If prompts live in a database with no history, that question has no answer.

## Structure that works

A reliable system prompt has five parts, in this order:

1. **Role and scope** — who the assistant is and what it covers.
2. **Grounding rules** — use only the supplied context; say when you cannot answer.
3. **Output format** — structure, citation style, length.
4. **Boundaries** — what never to do.
5. **Examples** — one or two, if behaviour is subtle.

Order matters. Models weight the beginning and the end most heavily, so critical constraints belong at the top and are worth restating at the bottom for long prompts.

## Specific beats polite

"Be helpful and accurate" changes nothing. "Answer only from the CONTEXT section. If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: 'I could not find that in the available documents.' Never use general knowledge." changes behaviour measurably.

## Delimiters and untrusted content

Always fence retrieved content and user input in clear delimiters, and state explicitly that anything inside them is data rather than instructions. This is your first line of defence against prompt injection — necessary, though not sufficient on its own.

## Version and measure

Store prompts as files in the repository with a version identifier. Record the version on every response. Run the evaluation set when a prompt changes. Without that loop you are changing behaviour by feel.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  P1[1. Role and scope] --> P2[2. Grounding rules]
  P2 --> P3[3. Output format]
  P3 --> P4[4. Boundaries]
  P4 --> P5[5. Examples if needed]
  P5 --> CTX[Context in delimiters\nmarked as data]
  CTX --> V[Version recorded\non every response]
keyTakeaways: Prompts are code: version them in the repository and record the version on every response
Specific instructions with exact refusal wording beat polite generalities
Fence retrieved content in delimiters and state explicitly that it is data, not instructions
Run the evaluation set whenever a prompt changes

lessons.title: Conversation Memory Inside a Token Budget
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The constraint

Models are stateless. Every request carries the whole conversation. A 40-turn conversation resent in full on turn 41 is expensive, slow and — because of mid-context degradation — often produces worse answers than a well-trimmed version.

## Four strategies

**Sliding window.** Keep the last N turns. Trivial, and it forgets the requirement stated in turn 2 that still matters in turn 40.

**Summarisation.** When history exceeds a threshold, summarise the older portion and keep recent turns verbatim. Costs an extra call; preserves the thread. This is the default for long assistant conversations.

**Structured extraction.** Pull durable facts — names, IDs, stated preferences, decisions — into a typed record carried separately from the transcript. The most reliable option when specific details must not be lost, and the most work.

**Retrieval over history.** Index past turns and retrieve the relevant ones. Best for very long-running relationships where most history is irrelevant to the current question.

Production systems combine them: a structured record of durable facts, a rolling summary of the middle, and the last few turns verbatim.

## Always budget explicitly

Decide the token allocation for history and enforce it. "It usually fits" fails on the day a user pastes a 30-page document into the chat.

## What to persist

Store the full transcript for audit and analysis; send only the budgeted view to the model. These are different concerns and conflating them is a common mistake.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  FULL[(Full transcript\npersisted for audit)] --> B[Context builder]
  B --> F[Durable facts\nstructured record]
  B --> S[Rolling summary\nof older turns]
  B --> R[Last 6 turns verbatim]
  F --> BUD{Within token budget?}
  S --> BUD
  R --> BUD
  BUD -->|Yes| SEND[Send to model]
  BUD -->|No| TRIM[Trim oldest verbatim turns]
  TRIM --> SEND
keyTakeaways: Models are stateless: every request resends the conversation, so history is a recurring cost
Combine durable facts, a rolling summary and recent verbatim turns
Enforce a token budget explicitly — "it usually fits" fails on a pasted document
Persist the full transcript for audit; send only the budgeted view to the model

modules.title: The RAG Pipeline and Chunking

lessons.title: The RAG Pipeline End to End
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The pipeline

```
Documents → Extraction → Chunking → Embeddings → Vector store
                                                      ↓
Question → Embedding → Hybrid search → Rerank → Context → LLM → Answer + citations
```

Two pipelines, really: ingestion (offline, batch, can be slow) and query (online, latency-critical). Keeping them separate in your design is the first structural decision.

## Where quality is won and lost

In practice the failure distribution is roughly:

- **60% retrieval.** The right chunk was never fetched. No prompt improves this.
- **25% chunking.** The right content was fetched but split so that the answer spans two chunks and neither is complete.
- **10% prompting.** The context was correct; the instruction was weak.
- **5% model.** Genuinely the model's limitation.

Teams consistently spend their time in reverse order to this distribution. When answers are poor, instrument retrieval first: log what was retrieved, its scores, and whether the correct document was present at all.

## Why naive RAG disappoints

A weekend prototype — fixed 1,000-character chunks, pure vector search, top 5, stuff into a prompt — works impressively on a demo corpus and disappoints on a real one. Real corpora have tables, headers, boilerplate, near-duplicate revisions, contradictory versions and identifiers that vectors handle poorly.

The gap between the two is exactly what this phase teaches.

## Design decisions to make explicitly

Chunk size and overlap. Metadata captured at ingestion. Hybrid versus pure vector. Reranking. Top-k. Citation format. Refusal threshold. Every one of these is a decision you should be able to defend with a measurement.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Ingestion[Ingestion: offline]
    D[Documents] --> X[Extract]
    X --> C[Chunk + metadata]
    C --> E[Embed]
    E --> V[(Vector + keyword index)]
  end
  subgraph Query[Query: online]
    Q[Question] --> QE[Embed]
    QE --> HS[Hybrid search\n+ permission filter]
    HS --> V
    HS --> RR[Rerank top 50 to 10]
    RR --> TH{Above relevance\nthreshold?}
    TH -->|No| REF[Refuse]
    TH -->|Yes| CTX[Build context]
    CTX --> L[LLM]
    L --> A[Answer + citations]
  end
keyTakeaways: Around 60% of RAG failures are retrieval failures — instrument retrieval before touching prompts
Retrieve wide, rerank narrow: 50 candidates down to 10 context chunks
Enforce permissions in the search query, never in the prompt
Refusal is a feature: below the relevance threshold, decline

lessons.title: Chunking Strategies That Survive Real Documents
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why chunking decides so much

Chunk too large and the embedding becomes a blur of several topics, retrieval gets imprecise, and you waste context. Chunk too small and the answer is split across chunks, none of which is retrievable on its own.

## The strategies

**Fixed size with overlap.** 800–1,200 characters with 10–15% overlap. The baseline: simple, predictable, and it will cut through the middle of a table.

**Recursive character splitting.** Split on paragraph, then sentence, then word, preferring the largest natural boundary that fits. Better, still structure-blind.

**Structure-aware.** Split on the document's own structure — markdown headings, PDF sections, Word styles — and carry the heading path into each chunk's metadata. Much better for technical and policy documents, where a heading is the strongest signal of what a passage is about.

**Semantic.** Split where the topic changes, detected by embedding similarity between adjacent sentences. Expensive at ingestion, occasionally worth it.

## What actually works in enterprise corpora

Structure-aware splitting with a size ceiling, and the heading path prepended to the chunk text. A chunk that begins "Employee Handbook > Leave > Parental Leave" embeds far more usefully than one starting mid-sentence.

## Tables, and the trap

Tables break every text splitter. A table split across chunks produces rows with no headers, which is worse than useless because it retrieves confidently and answers wrongly. Extract tables separately, keep each with its headers, and consider a short text summary of the table alongside the structured form.

## Metadata is not optional

Capture at ingestion: document ID, title, heading path, page or section, effective date, version, owner and ACL. Every one of these becomes a filter, a citation component, or a freshness signal. Adding them later means reindexing everything.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD

  P --> T{Is it a table?}
  T -->|Yes| TB[Keep whole, with headers]
  T -->|No| SZ{Paragraph fits\nin the budget?}
  SZ -->|Yes| ACC[Accumulate to target size]
  SZ -->|No| SENT[Split on sentences]
  ACC --> EM[Emit chunk with\nheading prefix + overlap]
  SENT --> EM
  TB --> EM
  EM --> MD[Attach metadata:\nid, page, version, date, ACL]
keyTakeaways: Prepend the heading path to every chunk — it is the cheapest large retrieval win available
Tables must never go through a text splitter: extract them with their headers intact
Target roughly 300 tokens with about 10–15% overlap, then measure on your own corpus
Capture metadata at ingestion; adding it later means reindexing everything

modules.title: Hybrid Search, Filtering and Reranking
modules.summary: Combining keyword and vector retrieval, filtering by metadata and entitlement, and reranking what comes back.

lessons.title: Hybrid Search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why neither alone is enough

Vector search finds meaning and misses exact terms. Keyword search finds exact terms and misses paraphrase. Real questions need both, often in the same sentence: *"what's the excess on policy P-4471 for water damage?"* contains an exact identifier and a semantic concept.

## Reciprocal rank fusion

The practical way to combine two ranked lists without needing comparable scores — which you do not have, because BM25 scores and cosine similarities are not on the same scale.

RRF uses **rank**, not score:

```
score(d) = Σ  1 / (k + rank_i(d))
```

with k typically 60. A document ranked first in both lists scores highest; a document ranked well in one and absent from the other still scores respectably. It is simple, parameter-light and robust — which is why it is the default in Azure AI Search and most search engines.

## Weighting

If your corpus is dominated by identifiers and codes, weight keyword higher. If it is prose, weight vector higher. Make it configurable and tune it against your evaluation set rather than by intuition.

## Query rewriting

Two cheap techniques that pay off:

- **Contextualisation.** "What about the deductible?" is meaningless standalone. Rewrite it using conversation history into "What is the deductible for water damage on policy P-4471?" before retrieval.
- **Multi-query.** Generate two or three phrasings, retrieve for each, fuse the results. Costs an extra small-model call and measurably improves recall.

## Measure it

Run your evaluation set with keyword only, vector only, and fused. The improvement is usually substantial — and occasionally it tells you your corpus only needs one of them, which is also worth knowing.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  Q[Question] --> RW[Rewrite using\nconversation history]
  RW --> V[Vector search top 50]
  RW --> K[Keyword search top 50]
  V --> F[Reciprocal rank fusion\nscore = Σ 1/(60 + rank)]
  K --> F
  F --> T[Top 50 fused candidates]
  T --> RR[Rerank]
keyTakeaways: Vector search misses exact identifiers; keyword search misses paraphrase — real questions need both
RRF fuses on rank, avoiding the incomparable-scores problem entirely
Rewrite follow-up questions using conversation history before retrieving
Carry the per-leg ranks through: they are how you diagnose retrieval problems

lessons.title: Metadata Filtering, Permissions and Reranking
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Filtering is a security control

Metadata filters do two jobs. They narrow the search — by date, department, document type, version. And they enforce entitlement.

The second is a hard rule: **permission filters must be applied in the retrieval query**. Retrieving everything and filtering afterwards means the content was loaded, may be logged, and is one bug away from the response. Telling the model "only use documents the user may see" is not a control at all — it is a request, and requests can be argued with.

## Freshness and versioning

Enterprise corpora contain superseded documents. Without a version or effective-date filter, retrieval happily returns the 2019 policy alongside the 2026 one, and the model has no way to know which governs. Filter to current versions by default; surface superseded ones only when explicitly asked.

## Reranking

First-stage retrieval is fast and coarse: it compares a query vector against document vectors that were computed independently. A cross-encoder reranker processes query and passage **together**, which is far more accurate — and far too slow to run over a whole index.

Hence: retrieve 50 cheaply, rerank to 10 accurately. This is typically the single largest quality improvement available after hybrid search, and it is usually a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

## Deduplication

Real corpora contain near-duplicates: the same policy in three formats, a document and its summary. Ten retrieved chunks saying the same thing waste the context budget. Deduplicate on content similarity before building the context.

## Know what it cost

Reranking adds latency — typically 100–300ms — and a per-call charge. Measure the quality gain on your evaluation set and decide deliberately. Sometimes the answer is to rerank only when the first-stage scores are close.

flowchart TD
  U[User + group claims] --> F[Build filter:\nACL + current version + date]
  Q[Question] --> S[Hybrid search WITH filter]
  F --> S
  S --> C[50 candidates\nall permitted]
  C --> RR[Cross-encoder rerank]
  RR --> D[Deduplicate near-identical]
  D --> CTX[10 context chunks]
  style F fill:#7f1d1d,color:#fff
keyTakeaways: Permission filters belong in the retrieval query; post-filtering is not a security control
Filter to current versions by default, or the model sees superseded and current policy together
Reranking is usually the largest quality gain after hybrid search

modules.title: Citations, Hallucination Reduction and Evaluation
modules.summary: Making answers traceable, making refusal reliable, and proving the pipeline got better rather than worse.

lessons.title: Citations and Hallucination Reduction
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Citations are a control, not decoration

A citation does three things: it lets the user verify the claim, it gives you a measurable groundedness signal, and it constrains the model's behaviour. Requiring a citation for every claim measurably reduces invention, because the model must tie each statement to supplied text.

## Making citations reliable

- Put an explicit marker on each context chunk: `[doc-id:page]`.
- Instruct the model to cite after every claim using exactly that marker.
- **Validate the citations returned.** Models occasionally cite a document that was not in the context. Parse the response, check each citation against the retrieved set, and drop or flag any that does not resolve.

That validation step is what separates a citation feature from a citation theatre.

## Refusal is a feature

The most valuable behaviour in an enterprise assistant is declining cleanly. Three layers make it reliable:

1. **Retrieval threshold.** If the best reranked score is below your floor, refuse before calling the model at all. Cheapest possible refusal.
2. **Prompt instruction.** Exact wording for the refusal, so it is recognisable and testable.
3. **Post-check.** If the answer has no valid citations and is not a refusal, treat it as a failure rather than shipping it.

## Other reductions that work

Low temperature — 0 to 0.2 — for factual answering. Never instruct the model to "use your knowledge if the context is insufficient"; that sentence converts a grounded system into an ungrounded one. And show retrieved sources in the UI so users can verify independently of whether the model cited well.

## Measuring groundedness

Split the answer into claims and ask a judge model whether each is supported by the retrieved context. Track the score release over release. A drop in groundedness is the earliest reliable signal that a change made things worse.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  Q[Question] --> R[Retrieve + rerank]
  R --> L1{Top score above\nthreshold?}
  L1 -->|No| REF[Refuse: no model call]
  L1 -->|Yes| GEN[Generate with\ncitation requirement]
  GEN --> PARSE[Parse citations]
  PARSE --> VAL{All resolve to\nretrieved context?}
  VAL -->|Some fabricated| LOG[Drop and log]
  VAL -->|None valid| REF
  VAL -->|Valid| ANS[Answer + verified citations]
  LOG --> ANS
keyTakeaways: Requiring a citation per claim measurably reduces invention
Validate every citation against the retrieved set — models occasionally cite what was never there

lessons.title: Evaluating and Tuning a RAG Pipeline
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Tune one thing at a time

A RAG pipeline has perhaps a dozen tunable parameters: chunk size, overlap, embedding model, candidate count, fusion weights, reranker, context count, relevance threshold, temperature, prompt version. Changing several at once tells you nothing about which change helped.

The discipline: fix an evaluation set, change one parameter, measure, record. It is slower than it feels like it should be and it is the only approach that converges.

## Order of tuning, by expected payoff

1. **Add hybrid search** if you have only vector search. Usually the largest single gain.
2. **Add reranking.** Usually the second largest.
3. **Fix chunking** — structure-aware with heading context.
4. **Tune candidate count and context count.** More context is not better past a point.
5. **Tune the relevance threshold** to balance refusals against wrong answers.
6. **Then** tune the prompt.

Most teams start at step 6 because it is the easiest to change, and then conclude that RAG does not work well.

## Building the evaluation set

Take real questions from logs or from the people who will use the system. Include: common questions, questions whose answers span two documents, questions with near-duplicate distractors in the corpus, and questions the corpus genuinely cannot answer. That last category is the one everyone forgets, and it is how you measure refusal behaviour.

Thirty to fifty cases is enough to detect meaningful regressions.

## Track over time

Store every evaluation run with its configuration. When quality drops three months from now, you want the history, not a re-derivation.
lessons.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  B[Baseline measurement] --> H[Add hybrid search]
  H --> R[Add reranking]
  R --> C[Fix chunking]
  C --> K[Tune candidate and context counts]
  K --> T[Tune relevance threshold]
  T --> P[Tune the prompt]
  P --> G[Gate CI on the score]
  style H fill:#065f46,color:#fff
  style R fill:#065f46,color:#fff
keyTakeaways: Change one parameter at a time or the measurement means nothing
Hybrid search and reranking usually outrank every prompt change available to you
More context is frequently worse as well as more expensive — measure it
Include unanswerable questions in the evaluation set; that is how refusal gets measured
